about: What a query's statement must be, on each engine: one statement that only reads. The runner (engine.QueryRefusal) and its caller's check of the same rule read these cases. cases hold on every engine, and engineCases on the engines they name. A case that is refused says why, by its code. sentences are what the rule says, word for word, for one case of each kind.

cases.note: One statement that only reads

cases.sql: WITH x AS (SELECT 1) SELECT * FROM x
SELECT 1 /*+ a hint is a comment */ FROM permits

cases.note: A word that writes inside quoted text, a quoted name or a comment is not a word
cases.sql: SELECT 'DELETE FROM t' AS note FROM t
SELECT 'a;b -- not a comment' FROM t

SELECT a -- DELETE it later
FROM t

SELECT permit_no -- a comment
FROM permits

SELECT id FROM permits WHERE note LIKE '%--%'
AND code = 'a;b'

cases.note: A word that writes inside a longer name is another word
cases.sql: SELECT created_at, updated_at, deleted_at, into_date, update_count FROM t

cases.note: A backslash that stands before no quote is only a backslash, and a sign is a sign
cases.sql: SELECT path FROM t WHERE path LIKE 'C:\%'

cases.note: A letter outside a to z is taken inside quotes and inside a comment
cases.sql: SELECT "straße", "名前" FROM permits WHERE applicant = 'Zoë' -- größer

cases.note: A number is a number

cases.sql: SELECT valuation * 1.2e1 AS v2 FROM permits

cases.note: Each engine's own quoting, and a word that one engine reserves
cases.sql: SELECT TOP 3 permit_no FROM permits ORDER BY issued OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY

cases.note: Nothing to run
Not a SELECT
More than one statement
A word that writes, wherever it stands

cases.sql: SELECT a FROM t INTO OUTFILE '/tmp/x'
WITH x AS (SELECT 1 AS a) DELETE FROM dbo.permits

cases.note: Text before the first SELECT. SQL Server runs a procedure named at the start of a batch with no EXEC, and quoted text is not a space, so it hides nothing in front of SELECT
A word that writes and touches a number. An engine reads 1e1DELETE as a number and then DELETE
A number that holds such a word is refused too, though it is only a number: it is written another way
cases.sql: SELECT permit_no FROM permits WHERE flags = 0xDBCC01

cases.note: Where a comment ends. Some engines end -- at a carriage return alone, some nest /* */, and MySQL runs /*! */

cases.sql: SELECT 1 -- xINTO permits_copy FROM permits

SELECT 1 -- it's a comment
; DROP TABLE t

cases.note: What is a quote, engine by engine. A statement that ends with --' was hidden from a check that took the quote for the start of a text

A bracket on MySQL. MySQL reads a bracket as no part of a statement, and a MariaDB server in MSSQL mode reads [name] as a quoted name, so on MySQL a bracket outside quotes is refused. Inside quoted text or a comment a bracket is text
cases.sql: SELECT permit_no FROM permits WHERE note = '[draft]'

cases.note: A $ that starts a word on MySQL. MySQL 8.1 and later read $$ or $tag$ there as the start of quoted text, which only a stored program's body may hold, so on MySQL such a $ is refused. Inside a name it is part of the name
cases.sql: SELECT permit_no, '$$' AS mark FROM permits

cases.note: An at sign. On SQL Server @ is part of a name and on MySQL it starts a variable. PostgreSQL reads it as an operator and Oracle as the start of a database link's name, so there a word ends at @ and the word after it is read by itself

cases.sql: SELECT permit_no FROM permits WHERE tags <@ other_tags

cases.note: A letter outside a to z that stands outside quotes. The engines do not agree on which of them are part of a name
cases.sql: WITH é$$ AS (DELETE FROM permits RETURNING 1) SELECT 1 FROM é$$
SELECT 1 AS é$$ FROM permits; DROP TABLE permits; SELECT 1 AS é$$

cases.note: A character that is not text

engineCases.note: A bracket on MySQL. MySQL reads a bracket as no part of a statement, and a MariaDB server in MSSQL mode reads [name] as a quoted name, so on MySQL a bracket outside quotes is refused. Inside quoted text or a comment a bracket is text

A $ that starts a word on MySQL. MySQL 8.1 and later read $$ or $tag$ there as the start of quoted text, which only a stored program's body may hold, so on MySQL such a $ is refused. Inside a name it is part of the name

An at sign. On SQL Server @ is part of a name and on MySQL it starts a variable. PostgreSQL reads it as an operator and Oracle as the start of a database link's name, so there a word ends at @ and the word after it is read by itself
A second statement with no semicolon. SQL Server reserves the word that starts it, and MySQL's LOCK IN SHARE MODE holds rows locked

sentences.says: A query holds no control character but a tab and a line end, and a line feed follows each carriage return.
A query's quotes, brackets and comments are closed.
A query writes a quote inside quoted text as two quotes, with no backslash before it.
A backtick quotes a name on MySQL only. On SQL Server, write the name in double quotes.
A query writes text between plain quotes: Oracle's q'[...]' form is not taken.
A query has no { outside quotes: SQL Server reads {call ...} as a call.
On MySQL a query has no [ outside quotes: a MariaDB server in MSSQL mode reads [name] as a quoted name. Write the name in backticks.
On MySQL a query has no $ at the start of a word: MySQL 8.1 and later read $$ or $tag$ there as the start of quoted text. A name that starts with $ is written in backticks.

sentences.sql: SELECT permit_no FROM permits WHERE valuation > $1
sentences.says: On PostgreSQL a $ outside quotes opens quoted text ($$...$$ or $tag$...$tag$), set apart from the word before it. A query has no parameters ($1).
A query has no # outside quotes: MySQL starts a comment there. A name that holds one is written in quotes.
A query's -- comment has a space after it.
A query has no comment MySQL would run (/*! ... */).
A query has no /* inside a comment: some databases nest comments and some do not.
Outside quotes, a query holds only the letters a to z, digits and signs. A name with another letter is written in quotes.
A query needs a SELECT statement.
A query reads: it starts with SELECT or WITH.
A query is one statement.
A query reads: SELECT INTO writes, so it does not run.
A query reads: COMMIT changes the database, so it does not run. A column of that name is quoted.
A query reads: on SQL Server, SET is no part of a statement that only reads, so it does not run. A column of that name is quoted.

sentences.sql: SELECT * FROM permits LOCK IN SHARE MODE
sentences.says: A query reads: on MySQL, LOCK is no part of a statement that only reads, so it does not run. A column of that name is quoted.
A query reads: the number 1E1DELETE holds DELETE, which a database can read as a number and then DELETE, so it does not run. Write the number another way.

sentences.sql: SELECT permit_no FROM permits WHERE flags = 0xDBCC01
sentences.says: A query reads: the number 0XDBCC01 holds DBCC, which a database can read as a number and then DBCC, so it does not run. Write the number another way.
